reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of the CNS
clinicalPearls: A benign, slow-growing intraventricular tumour (CNS WHO grade 1), most often found in middle-aged and older adults
Characteristically located in the fourth ventricle or the lateral ventricles, attached to the ventricular wall
Frequently an incidental finding at imaging or autopsy, as many are asymptomatic
Symptoms, when present, usually reflect obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid flow with hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure
Histology shows clusters of bland glial cells within a dense fibrillary matrix, often with microcystic change and little mitotic activity
Mixed subependymoma-ependymoma tumours can occur, and the ependymoma component determines behaviour
Observation is reasonable for asymptomatic lesions, while symptomatic tumours are usually cured by surgical resection
reference.pathophysiology: Subependymoma is a slow-growing, benign glial tumour thought to arise from the subependymal glial cells lining the ventricles, possibly from a mix of ependymal and astrocytic progenitor cells. It grows as a well-demarcated nodular mass projecting into the ventricular lumen and is composed of small clusters of uniform, cytologically bland cells embedded in an abundant fibrillary glial matrix, commonly with microcysts and calcification. Proliferative activity is very low, accounting for its indolent behaviour, and it lacks the aggressive molecular features seen in higher-grade ependymal tumours. Clinical problems arise mechanically when the tumour is large enough to impede cerebrospinal fluid circulation.
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced brain MRI to characterise the well-defined intraventricular mass
Assessment of ventricular size for obstructive hydrocephalus
MRI features distinguishing it from ependymoma (typically minimal enhancement)
Histopathology confirming bland glial clusters in a fibrillary matrix
Immunohistochemistry (GFAP positivity) to confirm glial origin
Serial imaging surveillance for incidental asymptomatic lesions
redFlags: Obstructive hydrocephalus with rising intracranial pressure requiring intervention
Sudden deterioration from acute cerebrospinal fluid obstruction
Atypical or contrast-avid features suggesting a mixed or higher-grade ependymal component
New brainstem signs from a fourth-ventricular mass
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent, as subependymoma is benign and slow-growing; complete surgical resection of a symptomatic tumour is generally curative, and incidental asymptomatic lesions can often simply be monitored. Recurrence after gross total resection is uncommon.
pitfalls: Over-treating an incidental, asymptomatic benign lesion
Misinterpreting a mixed subependymoma-ependymoma as pure subependymoma and underestimating recurrence risk
Attributing symptoms to the tumour when they are due to unrelated pathology
Failing to recognise and relieve obstructive hydrocephalus in a symptomatic case
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System
Louis DN et al. The 2021 WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System
management: Most subependymomas are asymptomatic and slow growing; treatment is rarely needed unless hydrocephalus or demonstrated growth occurs
Observation with serial surveillance MRI is the standard approach for an incidental, asymptomatic lesion, and histologic confirmation is not mandatory if imaging features are classic
Surgical resection is the definitive treatment when the lesion is symptomatic, causing hydrocephalus, raised intracranial pressure, or focal mass effect

The surgical goal is maximal safe resection, often achieving gross total resection and cure for benign well demarcated tumors, but safety takes priority over completeness near eloquent structures or cranial nerves
Acute obstructive hydrocephalus may require cerebrospinal fluid diversion such as ventriculostomy or shunting as an urgent or staged step alongside resection
No established role exists for radiotherapy or chemotherapy in pure subependymoma

If pathology reveals a mixed subependymoma-ependymoma tumor, the ependymoma component drives further management, and postoperative radiotherapy is an established adjunct for ependymoma after subtotal resection or higher grade histology
There are no defined lines of therapy; management is a single surgical decision point of observe versus resect, and recurrence after complete resection is uncommon
Patients under observation should have serial contrast enhanced brain MRI at intervals guided by baseline size, growth rate, and symptoms
Postoperative surveillance imaging is used to detect the uncommon recurrence after resection
Clinical monitoring for symptoms of raised intracranial pressure or new focal deficits should prompt earlier repeat imaging
Refer to neurosurgery when the lesion is symptomatic, causes hydrocephalus, or shows growth on surveillance
Refer to neuro-oncology if histology shows a mixed subependymoma-ependymoma tumor
Refer to neuroradiology or a tumor board when imaging is atypical, such as unexpected contrast enhancement, to exclude a higher grade ependymal tumor or alternative diagnosis
